translation: ...another, that of the moist and cold, and a third besides these, the dry and cold, and another, that of the dry together with the hot. Some of them, however, say that there is a certain mixture moist and cold at once, and another hot and dry at once, but not the moist and hot at once, nor the cold and dry at once; for it is not possible, they say, for moisture to coincide with a prevailing heat, nor dryness with cold: for the moisture is consumed by the heat when it prevails, and thus the body becomes hot and dry at once, whereas it remains unconcocted and unwrought in those bodies in which the heat is weak; so that it is necessary, when heat predominates, that dryness follow, and when cold prevails, that moisture accompany it. These men, then, have persuaded themselves on these grounds that all the [mixtures] of the... are two...

Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus too, have stated precisely what one must look to in supposing a nature to be either well-mixed or ill-mixed; but these men do not know even this, but when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and hot, or that the mixture of the child is moist and hot, they neither understand how these things are said, and they senselessly transfer the account to the seasons, as though it were the same thing, and not vastly different, for one's own mixture to be moist and hot or for that of the air surrounding us to be so; for it is neither the same thing, nor is the mixture of an animal said to be moist and hot in the same way as the mixture of air is said to be moist and hot. What the cause of all these things was I shall now relate, and I shall show clearly to those willing to apply their minds that small slips among the...

...left-handed, there is nothing absurd. So too, then, a dog is moist and dry at once, and hot and cold at once, but not in relation to the same thing: for in relation to a man he is dry, but moist in relation to an ant; and in relation to a man hot, but cold in relation to a lion. And indeed he is hot as being alive (for if something has died it is not hot), but not hot in relation to another dog, if it should so happen. All these things, then, are said in relation to one another by comparison; but things said as within the genus of animals are said in another manner, as again also according to the species of animal: for a dog, in relation to an ant and a bee, is moist, but as within the genus of animals he is dry; and among dogs themselves according to species, this one is dry, that one moist, and some other, as...

...of its nature is in the best condition is judged by its activities; for indeed we say that any plant or animal whatsoever is in the best condition at that time when it functions best. For the excellence of a fig tree is to bring to perfection the best and most figs; and in the same way that of the vine is to bear in abundance the most and finest grapes; of a horse, to run fastest; and of a dog, to be exceedingly spirited toward hunting and guarding, but gentlest toward its own household. All these things, then, I mean both the animals and the plants, we shall say have the best and middle mixture within their own genus, not simply when there is a precise equality of the opposites, but when the symmetry appropriate to its capacity is present. And we say that justice too is something of this kind: not the equal by weight and measure, but by what is fitting...

...for if he was inquiring, as within animals, of what mixture it was, one must make the answer itself looking to the mean of all animals in their mixture; but if simply and as in relation to all substance, then one must now compare the opposites within it to one another, and consider the mixture no longer by referring it to the activities but to the bulks of the elements. But if he asked by comparing it specifically with some particular thing, one must compare it with that alone; and still more so if we were asked, of some one of the individual substances, as for instance, say, Dion or this particular dog, what sort its mixture is, one must not answer simply; for from this the sophists get no small occasion for quibbling. For if you were to say that Dion is of a hot and dry mixture, it is easiest for him, having brought forward one of those drier and hotter than him, the...

...those of animals and those of plants and those of all inanimate things, such as bronze and iron and stones and timbers, are ranked in the interval between those primary ones; for none of them is extremely hot, nor extremely cold, nor extremely moist, nor extremely dry, but either it is precisely in the middle of the opposites, so as to be no more hot than cold, or dry than moist, or it has advanced toward one of the extremes, so as to be more hot than cold, or more moist than dry. If, then, it should be precisely in the middle with respect to each of the oppositions, so as to be no more hot than cold, or dry than moist, this will be called well-mixed simply; but if one has prevailed, whether in the one antithesis or in both, it is no longer well-mixed. If, then...

...the other antithesis, the soft nerve is no longer in the middle of hot and cold, but falls short of heat by just as much as it does of blood. And so too all the other things mentioned before are colder than skin by just so much as they are more bloodless; and the tunics themselves of the most blood-filled vessels, I mean artery and vein, are bloodless and cold by nature, but by the neighbourhood of the blood they are warmed and arrive at a middle state of mixture. The blood, in turn, itself has its warmth from the heart; for by nature that viscus is of all the parts of the animal the most full of blood and at the same time the hottest, and next after it the liver. But the heart falls a little short of skin in hardness, whereas the liver falls far short; and accordingly it is moister than skin by as much as it is softer. And indeed also...

...and in the movements of the limbs; he is always of good colour and breathes well, and is midway between the sleepy and the wakeful, between the bare of hair and the hairy, between the dark in complexion and the fair; and his hair, while he is a child, is more reddish than dark, but in his prime the reverse. Since we have also made mention of his difference according to the ages, it would be no worse now to say something about these too. I wished, then, first to go through the causes of each of the signs mentioned; but since the inquiry concerning the ages is more pressing for the present matters, and renders us best supplied for the discovery of the causes, we shall now undertake this. Let us consider, then, the animal just being formed in the wombs of those who bear it, so that we may learn how it is moistest and hottest; for its first constitution is from...

...the nurses of infants mould the limbs as if they were of wax: so great is the moisture in the whole body of children. But also, if you should wish either to eat a young sacrificial animal or to dissect and examine it, you will find the flesh mucous and flabby, and the whole bony kind resembling cheese that is just curdling; so that the bodies of newborn animals are not even pleasant to eat, owing to their excessive moisture. And this is most of all the case with the flesh of pigs and of sheep, because they are also most moist; whereas that of goats, because it is drier, is both better and more pleasant to eat. Contrary to young sacrificial animals, those that have grown old have all the bones and all their ligaments sufficiently dry and sapless and juiceless, and the flesh sinewy and hard, and the arteries and the...

...in the mouth a quantity of saliva collects; but they also cough and spit up phlegm, showing thereby that the lung too is full of such a humour; and their belly is filled with phlegm, and each of the joints is somewhat mucous. But none of these things contradicts the bodies of those growing old being dry; for the nerves and the arteries and the veins and the membranes and the tunics of all the organs you will find much drier than before, though there is plastered about them, both within and without, either some phlegmatic humour or a mucous moisture. But all such signs are so far from showing old age to be moist that they even seem to me to bear witness to its dryness; for it is on account of this very thing that each of the parts becomes drier, because it is no longer nourished in the same way, now through weakness of the heat, a quantity...

...it seems to me, since the pattern of the arguments is now clearly known from what we have said; for both parties reason from afar, and almost infer the prior things from the posterior, and make their argument as though the hearers already knew how growth, how concoction, and how nutrition come about; and likewise they go through sensation and motion and the practical and natural activities, and mention the genesis of sleep and the nature of foods, of which none is simply and easily knowable, but each requires a very great deal of inquiry, and perhaps cannot even be discovered unless one previously knew how to recognise a moist and a dry and a hot and a cold mixture. For whatever of those things they say, as though already knowing it, if someone were to compel them to demonstrate it, they will in every case need the account of mixtures which is now before us; so that through one another and...

...the present argument, one must not take their proofs from things not yet known, but, as is both correct and just, what is to be taken for the demonstration ought to be either one of the evident things or one of the things previously demonstrated. Neither, then, must one mention the genesis of sleep, nor concoction, nor growth, nor any other of such things, but let the inquiry proceed from the sole and bare substance of the matters under consideration, just as we also did throughout the first book. For having distinguished that what is in actuality is one thing and what is in potentiality another, we said that the account must first be made concerning what is already hot and cold and dry and moist in actuality, and then thus arrive at the things in potentiality. And ready to hand for all and familiar is the [knowledge] of things already hot in actuality...

...which posits principles and elements, to have strayed so far from the men who posited these as not to know that the principles of every demonstration are the things evident to sense and to thought, and that whoever is at a loss about these seeks in vain concerning the rest, having left himself no starting point whence to begin. Whence, then, they turned to so long a wandering and attempted to seek by reasoning the diagnosis of sensible things, I for my part cannot even conceive; and for this reason I judge by touch what is hot in actuality, while whatever is not yet hot but is suited to become such, which indeed is also called hot in potentiality, this I attempt to discover by reasoning. But with them everything has somehow been overturned, and a long rhetoric has been practised about the arguments. These men, then, let us leave aside, having reminded ourselves of just this much even now, that...

...nor is it reasonable at all to confirm the prior things from the posterior. Let us judge, then, by sensation the hot and cold body, that which is already such in actuality and no longer in potentiality, putting aside both the first judgement and all the other signs. And indeed I release you, as one who will judge well, to the test, while I myself shall explain my own judgement. For touching many bodies in succession with care, not of children only or of infants, but also of youths and of those in their prime, I found neither party speaking the truth, neither those who said the man in his prime is simply hotter than the child, nor those who said he is colder. For if, having removed all the other alterations from without, you should examine the differences arising from age alone, neither appears to you simply hotter; for it is in quality that their heats differ, with an unequal transpiration, on account of which also...

...the spinal [marrow] is of the same kind, whereas all the other marrows are of another nature. The brain is moister and hotter than the spinal marrow, and for this reason also softer; and indeed the front parts of the brain itself are moister by just as much as they are also softer. All these, however, are not only moister than skin but also colder; and in general everything bloodless is colder than what contains blood. Nearest to skin is also the nature of the soft nerves; while that of the hard ones is just like the skin itself, in respect of moisture, that is, and dryness, for in heat it falls short by as much as it is likely that what is entirely bloodless should fall short of a body containing blood. The flesh of the spleen and that of the kidneys and that of the liver is moister than skin by as much as it is also softer, and hotter by as much as it is also fuller of blood. And indeed the flesh of the heart too...

...both catarrhs and coughs and runnings of the nose and a quantity of saliva; for all these show it to be colder and moister, and still more so if upon chance occasions it falls into such conditions. Baldness, however, is upon dryness; and the growth of dark and abundant hair is a sign of good mixture of the brain. In this manner, then, one must always consider the question of mixture, examining each part separately, and not venture to pronounce about all from one, as some have done, saying that the snub-nosed are moist and the hook-nosed dry, and those whose eyes are small dry, and those whose eyes are large moist. On this point, indeed, they are even at variance among themselves: for some, having assumed that the eyes are among the moist parts, in those in whom they find them larger [infer] moisture of mixture in...

...the same thing, either to evacuate some moisture of a thing dispersed in certain regions, or to render its proper mixture drier; for a certain uneven bad-mixture comes about in the inflamed parts, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their proper nature but still changing and being altered, while all the intervening spaces are filled with the flux. All things, then, that are hot and moist in mixture, applied to those so disposed, evacuate that superfluity which has occupied the spaces between the homoeomerous parts, but are so far from drying the bodies themselves that they even impart moisture to them. The truth, then, stands thus; but what has been said needs a demonstration, which, considering it to be longer than could be appended to the present discussion, and moreover requiring a hearer who understands the faculties of drugs, I defer, at least for...

...if you wish, the yellow bile, and that all the other things are hot accidentally, by partaking of these, will it not be necessary that the animal become hotter in two ways, either by acquiring more hot humours, or by having them hotter than before? To me at least it seems entirely so. And in the same manner, I think, it will also be colder in two ways, either by the cold humours, such as phlegm and black bile, having been bred in greater quantity, or by the quality alone having been altered while the symmetry of them all remains. What wonder is it, then, that so long as food cold by nature, such as purslane and lettuce, is being concocted, the body is filled with a cold quality, but when it has been concocted thoroughly and has become good blood, the body becomes in turn hotter than it was, by the generation of the hot humour? And indeed...

...the condition, if it is simple and one, while the judgement is determined by time, in the following way: what appears evidently to cool or to heat at the very moment of its application would surely be such both in itself and through itself; whereas what does so in the course of time might perhaps be brought to this from some accident, just as, in tetanus, in midsummer, for a young man of good flesh, an affusion of much cold water produces a recall of heat. But that the cold water does not heat in itself is clear from the first impact: for it produces a sensation of cooling, and indeed it also cools the skin so long as it is being poured over it; and the warmth it furnishes neither in all bodies nor during the affusion itself, but only in young men of good flesh, in midsummer, after one has stopped pouring. Just as, then, those upon whom there falls...

...of the ease and the benefit, this is of necessity cold, [even if] on others it sometimes appears hot; for it will be found, when examined precisely in those cases, not heating in itself but by some accident. And when we say in itself, or primarily, or through none of the intermediates, the same thing is signified in effect by all these expressions; and the exercise of all these together with their proper examples we shall carry out in the commentaries on drugs. But now, having again recalled what I have already said before, I shall try to set upon the present discussion its fitting conclusion. For since the hot body was spoken of in many ways, for there is both that which has the extreme quality, the element itself, and that which is named by its predominance, and further that which is said in relation to another, either to the well-proportioned member of the same genus, or to anything whatsoever...

...and indeed with rose cerate it helps greatly for those conditions; for which, and for such conditions, many other drugs too will be described in the following discussion, some having a power similar to the phoenicine, some even more active. But for rheumatic affections this is the best drug of all, and it has often accomplished something beyond hope. Once, then, when a thigh had suppurated near the groin, the inflammation throughout the whole of it being unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors should flow out toward the groin through the ulcer that had formed; and when this had taken place over a longer time, the flux that had descended into the thigh was evacuated, but a fistulous condition arose beneath the skin along the whole thigh, so that I wished to cut it open near the kneecap, in order that there might be an outflow for the ichors on either side...

...having taken in addition vinegar; for that one is useful on every occasion, whereas the white one made with pepper is useful for burns that have been stripped of skin when they are being brought to a scar, but earlier, by itself, it is useless, though when dissolved in myrtle oil it is useful, not however with equal strength to the drugs that are specifically suited for burns. And Heras says that it is suited for bites; but here too there is need of a distinction: for in the hard and hard-to-concoct cases the drug is too weak, whereas in the more moderate ones it is sufficient, and especially in old men and children and women, and, to speak summarily, in those of tender flesh. The drug is useful also for pimples, as Heras wrote this too truthfully; but he pronounced without distinction concerning eruptions: for of these too it treats those that are moderately somewhat hard, but those...

...but the measure is not equal to the Roman; for different people use a different sextarius measure. Among the Romans, at any rate, the sextarius holds one litra and a half and a sixth, so that the total is 20 ounces, which they generally measure by horns incised on the outside with certain circular lines. But some have falsely supposed that the Roman sextarius holds eighteen metric ounces. It seems, then, that Heras too, when he writes cotyle, signifies the half of the sextarius; but whether they mean the 9 ounces from the litra-horn or the ten, this is unclear. And whether it is also a suitable drug for those bitten by rabid animals, whether swallowed or applied externally, it is not possible to know from reasoning; for it has been shown by us that such drugs have their action through the whole peculiarity of their substance...

...concerning nourishment, that the bad and the not-bad are spoken of among relative terms, and evidently the harmful and the beneficial. For in another sense you would say that the Attalic plaster is better than this plaster, in that it is more widely useful. Indeed Asclepiades himself, writing it next after the one now described, does not name that very one, the plaster with white pepper, Attalic but Pamphilion, being ignorant, as I think, of the man who first discovered it, and having attached the name of the one who used it and gave it to him. At any rate he wrote its profession word for word thus: Another, called Pamphilion, a well-tried drug; it acts upon old and hard-to-heal [ulcers], carbuncles, epinyctides, achores, scabby conditions; it closes up sinuses; it acts upon abscesses, condylomata; and the drug is almost more widely useful. He says it is composed of white lead...

...let each of these be [done] precisely, for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. And concerning the white lead it has been said before, and the oil, and the manner of the boiling, and the surrounding air, and the fire, how each of them may contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the case of the others, so also in these one must, knowing the powers of water and of vinegar and of sea-water and of the whitest wine, mix into the composition the one most useful for the condition being treated. For in the case of callous-rimmed ulcers, which have their lips thick and hard and in need of much attenuation, the [metallics] levigated with vinegar and sea-water are more useful than those with water; but in those cases where the fluid borne in the ulcers is acrid and biting, one must rather levigate in water...

...each of the metallics, just as again rather in wine in those cases where the fluid flowing into the ulcers appears abundant. Each of these, then, which I have mentioned, levigated over several days in each of the liquids named, I put on each occasion into the drugs made with white lead and litharge, and I found all of them cicatrising excellently; and I also gave some of the recipes to friends who asked for such drugs, by whom too, when brought to the test, they appeared to preserve their profession. So when the litharge has been boiled beforehand, as has been said, with the white lead, and the drug has come near to a non-staining consistency, one must add the larch resin or the terebinth resin together with the white wax, and when these have been well united, add in the metallics, having the following proportion: of litharge and of white lead, as is customary, a litra of each; let it be boiled with two litrai of oil, often...

...but if something scirrhous of its inflammation should be left behind, to apply some of the drugs that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something appeared to be lacking, I first used the drug made with the root of dracontium, which has all the rest the same as the Egyptian drug called Isis, but has taken in addition the root of dracontium; and next after this, having used the one called Athena, from that I passed, for the remainder, to the cicatrising drugs. In another case, smearing the denuded parts of the wound with the troche made with boiled-down must, dissolved, I applied externally the euphorbium, having mixed it with wax and resin in such a quantity that it should at once become plaster-like and preserve the power of the euphorbium. How one, looking to these aims, might compose the drug, I shall say next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar...

...just as to the resin and to the pitch; for this reason I mix into the cerate resin or pitch or a portion of each. It is quite clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them; for wax requires much of the fat for moistness, whereas of the resins the dry ones need very little indeed, and the moist ones even want to take on some dry substance for a plaster-like consistency. Among waxes, then, the difference in respect of moistness and dryness is not great; but with the resins, on the contrary, as also with pitch, the difference between the dry and the moist ones is very great. The driest of the resins, then, is the one which some call fried [resin] and others colophony; second is the one from the potteries, unpurified and unfried; but if one purifies it...

...[joining] me in the operation, some of those inexperienced in anatomy, doing the same thing, flay away from all the muscles the underlying membranes, not knowing that these may be stitched together with the muscles without danger, whereas it is most dangerous [to stitch] the tendons that have been flattened out like them. But however much they may be flattened, they are nevertheless still both thicker than the membranes and harder. You will see sufficiently thin tendons also in all the muscles along the epigastrium, except for the two straight ones, upon which the membranous aponeuroses of the oblique ones are laid; but no other tendon besides those mentioned is flattened out membranously, for all those that are flattened preserve a sufficient thickness so as to escape no one. The sympathy, however, of the overlying parts, as far as the very origin of the nerves, is no less in the muscles at the end of the thigh and in those inserting into the elbow of the forearm, and in those...

...you have seen me doing throughout, not with this alone but also with ammoniac incense. There is also the drug written after this one by the Tarentine, of the same profession, according to the following proportion: of chalcitis 25 drachmas, of cadmia 12 drachmas; having levigated them separately and mixed in unadulterated wine and boiled it, pour it over so that they are kneaded in due measure; then levigate until it is dried; and having melted 50 drachmas of wax, 30 drachmas of terebinth resin, 8 cotylae of myrtle oil, mix into the cerate 20 drachmas of the dry ingredients. And this drug has none of the emollient substances; however, in the mixing with the cerate, the one trained in reasoning in the methods I have set out would appropriately work out the fitting quantity of the mixture for each of the ulcers. And rightly too [he says] the unadulterated wine, that is, that with which sea-water has not been mixed...

...the meltable ingredients, having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ones upon these, stirring carefully. One must have, ground with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax; and into these are put the things in the pan, and they are ground so that lumps of wax do not form; and when it is in good order, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared it with iris oil. On the third kind of ulcers hard to treat, concerning which Asclepiades wrote word for word as follows: For ulcers that do not close at all, or that close but break down again, either the flesh being corrupted or even the underlying bones being destroyed, one must use the following preparations. For Chironian and hard-to-heal ulcers, a well-tried drug: of scale of copper, of scraped verdigris, one ounce each; of wax half a litra; of larch resin one ounce and a half. [Pour] the meltable ingredients over the dry ones, and having taken it up, use it, kneading it carefully and laying a small flat piece upon...

...the metallics with vinegar, and after these adding in the dry ingredients and levigating again; then, when these have a clay-like consistency, mixing in the meltable ingredients as has been said before. Another: of bitumen and of terebinth resin and of Bruttian pitch, one litra each; of oil 24 drachmas; of litharge and of white lead and of manna and of verdigris and of scale and of opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachmas of the oil; of ladanum two ounces, which is 16 drachmas; and two cotylae of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another: of chrysocolla and of scale and of steel, 4 drachmas each; of verdigris and of chalcanthum, the half of each, that is 2 drachmas each; of wax 25 drachmas, that is 3 ounces and one drachma; of terebinth resin 2 ounces, that is 16 drachmas. Melt the wax with the terebinth...

...it checks haemorrhoids and acts excellently in affections about the bladder. It contains: of frankincense 4 drachmas, of myrrh 4 drachmas, of saffron 4 drachmas, of Illyrian iris 4 drachmas, of bdellium 4 drachmas, of scale 12 drachmas, of chalcanthum 4 drachmas, of split alum 4 drachmas, of round [alum] 4 drachmas, of ammoniac incense 4 drachmas, of misy 4 drachmas, of rind of sweet pomegranate 4 drachmas, of aristolochia and of omphacitis gall-nut 8 drachmas each (otherwise 16), of chalcitis 4 drachmas, of ammoniac incense 4 drachmas, of oak mistletoe 8 drachmas, of opopanax 8 drachmas, of scraped verdigris 8 drachmas, of acacia 8 drachmas, of flower of roses 8 drachmas, of terebinth 1 mina (others say 50 drachmas), of poppy juice 6 drachmas, of wax 2 minae (others say 4 drachmas), of calf suet, prepared, 1 mina (others say 150), of common vinegar 2 cotylae, of wine [enough] for the dry ingredients. These...

...of verdigris of copper and of Indian aloe, of burnt copper and of good diphryges, sixteen and a half from each ingredient; twenty drachmas of galbanum, and 4 [more]; of manna of frankincense the same, twice 12; of ammoniac twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachmas of Attic propolis; of the long aristolochia twice 10 drachmas; twice 6 drachmas of scale of Cyprian copper; and of the driest root of gentian an equal amount. To all these add in addition of dittany herb, dry, bearing its flower, 20 holkai, ground fine. Having put litharge with oil into a new, broad-mouthed earthenware pan, boil over a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it acquires the thickness of Attic honey; and having added an equal amount of the scale as well, boil again more vigorously; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, and making the drug non-staining and set, add the wax and the...

...but of iris; and in place of the molybdaena put in two parts of litharge, and of the rest one part each. A dry septic of Lecanius Areius: of arsenic one litra, of quicklime 2 drachmas; grind in water for 30 days, changing the water twice a day, in the sun; then, having dried it out, use it. A sitz-bath for haemorrhoids, that of Phanias: of chalcanthum, of split alum, of chalcitis, of raw misy, of sandarach, 4 drachmas each; have them all finely ground. At the time of use put old, stale urine of a single man, in measure 2 sextarii, into an earthenware basin, and 12 drachmas of the drug; pour in the urine in addition so that the two sextarii are always kept up. Use this, sitting in it for 7 days, for in these it is effective; and when it becomes glutinous, smear the anus round with the sediment. A dry [powder] that cicatrises flesh, non-biting, according to Harpocras: of sandarach, of chrysocolla, of arsenic, an equal amount of each...

...of wax, nor the other of these; but the ammoniac incense alone, put in, will make the drug dry and harsh. But for plaster-making, for it is no worse to name it so, both the wax and the resin are useful; for the softening and dispersing belong to the drug from the ammoniac alone, which holds first place among emollients and is a rival also to the discutients. And having recalled what was said in the fifth book of the Powers of Simple Drugs, as to what sort the mixture must be for such drugs, you will no longer need any newer instruction; for the primary active powers in drugs lie in heat and cold and moisture and dryness, and the secondary ones are the emollient and discutient and repellent and attractive and concocting and detergent and septic, just as also...

...of all, carefully; again let a little drip off; [if] you see it of good colour and well blended, take the pot at once from the fire, and add galbanum, previously softened. But if the drug is by far too hard, add oil to it for a good blending. Having strained it thus, then into another vessel, cold, knead it with the hands and so store it away. I shall subjoin another, of the same kind as the one before this; it acts upon the affections I mentioned before: this one cicatrises better than all drugs ulcers hard to heal and callous and chronic; the eruptions arising on the face this one cures without any harmful biting; and seats having fissures and hardnesses of condyloma-like sort, and calluses, it casts off. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge (a mina is a litra and a third part of a litra); of good Pontic wax half a mina; of good scraped verdigris a fourth part of a mina...

...scrofulous swellings; reducing every oedema, and curing the watery conditions of the liver and of the spleen; bringing on copious excretions of urine; and it loosens sciaticas, even those become chronic. Ulpianus, a well-endowed young man, using this, benefited very many. It contains one litra of Pontic wax, one of fried [resin] and one of pine resin, of fresh quicklime 1 ounce, of split alum 1 ounce, and an amount equal to one of these of Pontic arsenic. Having poured over these a little fragrant vinegar, grind for a sufficient time in a larger mortar; and having added a little oil to wax and resin, melting it over a fire of vigorous flame, and mixing everything carefully, and making malagmata, keep it stored, having the thickness of a non-staining [plaster], using it, where needed, as a fresh compress. And Cratistus, the father of the drug, said also that for deliverance from long diseases...

...which also cure small inflammations. Of the compound emollients, some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first rank; some not much stronger than these, in the second; and certain others in the third; and besides these, others in the fourth. One ought to use them, as has been said before, for slight hardnesses and soft bodies those of the first rank, and for bodies and affections stronger than these those of the second, just as also those of the third and the fourth analogously. They subjoin also those under each of them separately. Emollient drugs of the first rank: butter, or Colophonian resin and white wax, not old, the 3 equal in weight, melted together, are emollients of the first rank; and so too the moist [resin] when it is fresh...

Menecrates did this because it often happens that errors are made in the writings not only by people unintentionally, but also intentionally, out of envy, by some, who make the letter omicron a theta by drawing another transverse line through the middle of the round line, and the letter iota [a tau] by similarly adding another transverse line; just as also, when one line has been scraped off from the letter [gamma] and from rho, it happens that the character of iota is left. In the same manner, out of many letters, by the addition of some, the combination of others, and the removal of others, it happens that the alteration of the characters that signify them comes about. But Menecrates accomplished nothing more for the subsequent time, since those who copied his book did not write the names of the numbers in full letters but by means of the characters that signify them.
